30.0.0.en: 1 "But now they that are younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock. 2 Yea, whereto might the strength of their hands profit me, in whom old age was perished? 3 For want and famine they were solitary; fleeing into the wilderness in former time desolate and waste. 4 Who cut up mallows by the bushes, and juniper roots for their meat. 5 They were driven forth from among men, (they cried after them as after a thief;) 6 To dwell in the cliffs of the valleys, in caves of the earth, and in the rocks. 7 Among the bushes they brayed; under the nettles they were gathered together. 8 They were children of fools, yea, children of base men: they were viler than the earth.

30.0.1.en: "But now they that are younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock" [1].

30.0.2.en: Job lived his life in perfection and uprightness, fearing God and eschewing evil (Job 1:1), and God Himself bore witness concerning him: "there is none like him in the earth" (Job 1:8). Perhaps in his old age he expected to serve others through his long experience, but he was surprised that instead of serving he became a laughingstock and a stumbling block to those around him, even to the wicked.

30.0.3.en: He felt as though everything he had practiced from his youth until his old age had passed like vapor without benefit, and that there was no cause before him to justify what he had reached. He almost collapsed completely in his soul, besides his collapse in body, in society and in property. This is what drove him to utter a bitter lamentation.

30.0.4.en: By saying "they that are younger than I" he does not mean only those who are younger than he in age, but also those who are less than he in knowledge, wisdom, experience, social standing and conduct. In this he does not mean his three friends alone, but all who came, even from afar, not to comfort him or to pray for him, but to despise him and mock him.

30.0.5.en: Since dogs were regarded at that time as unclean (1 Sam 17:43; Prov 26:11), Job considered the dogs of his flock to be cleaner than their fathers.

30.0.6.en: They insulted him in his old age and without cause, although honoring the elderly is counted as offered to God Himself. Holy Scripture requires us to respect the elderly, though it befits the elderly to bear in mind that true grey hairs are not in advanced age, but in wisdom and maturity. The commandment came: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the Lord" (Lev 19:32). [My son, help thy father in his age, and grieve him not as long as he liveth] (Sir 3:14). "Despise not a man in his old age: for even some of us wax old" (Sir 8:7).

30.0.7.en: We should not be amazed at the bitterness that righteous Job suffered, for the godly have suffered from many. For example, Paul suffered the bitterness of affliction until he almost despaired of his life, as he says: [We were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life: but we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead: who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us] (2 Cor 1:8-10).

30.0.8.en: * Paul was expecting death, but it did not happen. According to the natural course of events he should have died, but God did not yet allow it, so that Paul might learn not to trust in himself, but in God.

30.0.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * If the Apostles suffered, how much more does it befit others to suffer as they did.

30.0.10.en: Severian, Bishop of Gabala Yea, whereto might the strength of their hands profit me?

30.1.0.en: In whom old age was perished [2].

30.1.1.en: In bitterness Job looks at those coming to him, who mock him in his old age. In his youth he used to support the like of them, help them and serve them with love. Now they come to him in his old age, without strength or ability, and yet they think they have come to support him. Sadly, even in their presence they offered him what shatters him, not what helps him.

30.1.2.en: Perhaps, besides their poverty and lack of wisdom, they were old men unable to work, so that their coming to him was of no use. Some, however, think that he is speaking of the young men who mock him: if their elderly fathers did not take a fitting stand to comfort him, could their sons comfort him with a kind word that supports him? Their elderly fathers were harsh with him and heaped false accusations upon him, so will their sons offer comfort? Will they stretch out their hands to strengthen him in his ordeal?

30.2.0.en: "For want and famine (and hunger) they were solitary; fleeing into the wilderness in former time desolate and waste" [3].

30.2.1.en: Job portrays for us the state of those gathered around him, not to comfort him, but to mock him. They suffer from poverty and hunger until they have become extremely gaunt, like dry trees with no life and no fruit. They are people with no role in life, whom society has cast out because of their extreme recklessness and their lack of commitment to any work, so they have become like fugitives in the wilderness, where there is ruin and destruction. It is as though they have found their opportunity to project onto Job what they are within themselves.

30.2.2.en: This is what hatred does in them: it puts them in want, hunger and ruin, and even brings them into death while they are alive in the body.

30.2.3.en: * Our life is love; if life is love, then death is hatred.

30.3.0.en: St. Augustine Who cut up mallows by the bushes, and juniper roots for their meat [4].

30.3.1.en: Righteous Job portrays those who opposed him as people who find nothing to eat, and so resort to the mallow, a salty plant that the poor gather from among the bushes (such as the wormwood) to eat; and the broom, a tree whose flowers are like the lupine and whose seeds are like lentils. Some think that the broom here refers to bitter roots that the poor eat.

30.3.2.en: Such as these, whom Job used to feed and for whom he generously supplied their needs, came to him gloating over what he had come to.

30.3.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great), who was greatly influenced by the Fathers of the East, especially the writings of the Fathers of the Alexandrian and Cappadocian schools, sees these hungry poor as those who are content with the bark of the tree and not its fruit. They are content with the literal interpretation of Holy Scripture, without enjoying the fruits of the Spirit that satisfy the soul.

30.3.4.en: * [Those who are disturbed by desolation and misery and chew herbs and the bark of trees] [3, 4]... False teachers draw their followers into the same wilderness, as the Truth warned us before: "If they shall say unto you, Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth" (Mt 26:24). They deserve contempt for the desolation of their practice and the evil of their ideas...

30.3.5.en: [Eating herbs] in Holy Scripture signifies attending to the smallest commandments and neglecting the greatest of them. The Truth says: "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law (judgment, mercy, and faith)" (Mt 23:23).

30.3.6.en: These also eat the bark of trees, because in the Holy Scriptures they care for what is outward, that is, the letter, and take no heed of the spiritual meaning. They suppose that there is nothing else in the words of God except what is on the surface. Therefore the passion of vainglory possesses them, and with all their errors they thirst for the honor that holds them captive. In all that they say they seek nothing but earthly gain. Concerning this Paul says: "For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly" (Rom 18:16).

30.3.8.en: * Both Jews and Christians believe that Holy Scripture was written by the Holy Spirit, but we differ in the interpretation of what it contains. We do not live as the Jews do, because we believe that the literal interpretation of the Law does not carry with it the spirit of the Law.

30.3.9.en: * If God and the Lord is Spirit, we must hear in a spiritual way what the Spirit says to us.

30.3.10.en: Origen the Scholar * The Law is perfect and imperfect at the same time: it is perfect if we understand it spiritually (because it speaks to us of the mystery of Christ), but it is also imperfect if the mind of the people who come under its guidance does not go beyond the letter. For the material of the letter is only half of knowledge.

30.3.11.en: St. Cyril the Great They were driven forth from among men.

30.4.0.en: They cried after them as after a thief [5].

30.4.1.en: Righteous Job is amazed to see around him idle people whom society has cast out from among men, so that they fled from the cities like thieves. People considered them unworthy to live in a civilized and ordered society, and used to cry out after them, proclaiming that they were thieves. Instead of examining themselves and their faults, these came to mock Job.

30.5.0.en: To dwell in the cliffs of the valleys, in caves of the earth, and in the rocks [6].

30.5.1.en: Since Job was a ruler and judge, he used to consider with the elders of the city the great cases, such as dealing with vagrants who endangered security. Some of them would flee from the city and seek out caves in the midst of uninhabited valleys and mountains, living in them out of sight of the judiciary. Now, when they heard about Job and what had become of him, they thought he had become a vagrant like them, with no shelter and no one to receive him or comfort him, so they came to mock him as the most wretched of them.

30.5.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) and others see that they represent those who have no place in the city of God, dwelling as it were in the wildernesses and among the rocks in caves, in fearful regions. What occupies them is not a return to God but the mockery of the men of God and His saints.

30.5.3.en: They chose for themselves misery, gloom, isolation and bitterness, and what they think about is gloating over the suffering righteous. What delights their hearts is not that they enjoy good things, but that others be struck with evils and calamities. This is the work of the spirit of enmity, with hatred and malice. What occupies the mind of the malicious is the destruction of his brethren, not his own edification.

30.5.4.en: He who isolates himself from the Church of the Lord Christ is like one who has deprived himself of the spiritual paradise to live in the midst of the desolation of the wildernesses, and so he cannot take part in the song of the Church: "Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits" (Song 4:16); "My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies" (Song 6:2).

30.5.5.en: * "Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits" (Song 16:4). It is a bold expression from a soul full of enthusiasm and awe that rises above all wonder. Whom does the bride invite to her banquet, which consists of her own fruit? For whom does the bride prepare her banquet, which she has set from her own resources? Whom does the bride invite to eat of what she has set before him? [Of whom, and through whom, and to whom are all things] (Rom 36:11). He gives every person his meat in due season (Ps 15:145), He opens His hand and fills every living thing with plenty. He is the Bread that came down from heaven (Jn 41:6), He who gives life to the world and makes the waters overflow from His own spring for life. This is the One for whom the bride arranges her table. She is the garden from which living trees spring up. The trees signify us, and our saved spirits indicate the food offered to Him. And He said to His disciples: "I have meat to eat that ye know not of" (Jn 32:4, 34). It is the fulfillment of the holy will of God: [Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth] (1 Tim 4:2). This salvation, then, is the food that is prepared for Him. Our free will gives the fruit to God, which is our spirits, for Him to gather from their small branches. At the beginning the bride enjoyed the fruit of the apple tree, sweet to the taste, saying: "his fruit was sweet to my taste" (Song 3:2). Then she herself became the beautiful, sweet fruit that was offered to the Shepherd to enjoy.

30.5.6.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa Among the bushes they brayed.

30.6.0.en: Under the nettles they were gathered together [7].

30.6.1.en: Righteous Job portrays the wicked and malicious who have come to mock him as wild asses that live in the wilderness; when they gather together among the shrubs they bray with a harsh tone that is repulsive to the soul. That is, they have become like wild beasts that gather together to bray, seeking food for themselves, which is harming others and afflicting them with disasters.

30.6.2.en: They crowd together under the thorn bush where they seek shelter, and they stumble among the thorns of hatred and the briers of malice without cause.

30.6.3.en: In other words, even in the gathering of the wicked together, what they enjoy is savagery and animal behavior, without reason or balance, along with the bitterness of the choking thorns of sin.

30.6.4.en: * They are counted as those who crowd together under thorns, since they lift up their audacious thought to rejoice in the very things by which they carry the thorns of sins.

30.6.6.en: * Envy is a kind of drone (the male bee) that spoils the works of others and has no desire to raise itself, but is made to weep by the success of others, and so does everything in its power to bring them down.

30.6.7.en: What is this spirit like? It is like a dull, heavy-bodied ass yoked with a good horse. It does not want to advance, and at the same time with the weight of its body it keeps the horse from walking. So the envious man does not care how to be rid of this nightmare, but works with all his effort to bring down the one who desires to ascend to heaven, and in this he is exactly like Satan. If he sees a man in paradise, instead of correcting himself he seeks to cast the other out of paradise. And if he sees him seated in heaven while the others hasten toward rest, he uses the same plan, depriving them of going to it, and so brings upon himself a more severe fire.

30.6.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * The malicious man gains from his prayer what the sower gains from the harvest in the sea. As the ray of fire cannot be prevented from rising upward, so the prayers of the merciful cannot fail to ascend to heaven. As the flow of water runs downward, so is the power of anger once it has found a place in our mind.

30.6.9.en: * He who has found envy has found with him Satan, who brought it into being from of old.

30.7.0.en: St. Mar Isaac the Syrian They were children of fools, yea, children of base men: they were viler than the earth (or: they were driven out of the land) [8].

30.7.1.en: Since they are bound to ignorance and folly, they are counted children of folly instead of being children of men, and since they carry hatred and malice, the earth drives them out, and they become wanderers in the wilderness with no place in which to settle.

30.7.2.en: * "They are called children," not because they are born of their seed, but by imitating those who teach false doctrines; they are fools by reason of ignorance, and they lead an evil life like degraded men because of their conduct... Therefore he rightly continues: [And upon the earth they shall not appear at all]. Although they aim to show something, they surely become driven out of the land of the living.

30.8.s.en: 2. The lowliness of those who despise him

30.8.0.en: 9 "And now am I their song, yea, I am their byword. 10 They abhor me, they flee far from me, and spare not to spit in my face. 11 Because he hath loosed my cord, and afflicted me, they have also let loose the bridle before me. 12 Upon my right hand rise the youth; they push away my feet, and they raise up against me the ways of their destruction. 13 They mar my path, they set forward my calamity, they have no helper. 14 They came upon me as a wide breaking in of waters: in the desolation they rolled themselves upon me. 15 Terrors are turned upon me: they pursue my soul as the wind: and my welfare passeth away as a cloud.

30.8.1.en: "And now am I their song, yea, I am their byword" [9].

30.8.2.en: The wicked often mock the righteous and count them a byword of shame, just as God sometimes allows His people to become a byword among the peoples in order to discipline them.

30.8.3.en: "Thou makest us a byword among the heathen, a shaking of the head among the people" (Ps 44:14).

30.8.4.en: "I made sackcloth also my garment; and I became a proverb to them" (Ps 69:11).

30.8.5.en: "And they repenting and groaning for anguish of spirit shall say within themselves, This was he, whom we had sometimes in derision, and a proverb of reproach" (Wis 5:3).

30.8.6.en: "And I will deliver them to be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth for their hurt, to be a reproach and a proverb, a taunt and a curse, in all places whither I shall drive them" (Jer 24:9).

30.8.7.en: "Let the priests, the ministers of the Lord, weep between the porch and the altar, and let them say, Spare thy people, O Lord, and give not thine heritage to reproach, that the heathen should rule over them: wherefore should they say among the people, Where is their God?" (Joel 2:17).

30.8.8.en: * Behold, you see what affected him most: to see himself made the object of mockery, most of all by those whom he rebukes for the evil they practice.

30.8.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * Every person is despised on account of his righteousness; the more he qualifies for praise, the more he becomes an object of disgust to others.

30.9.0.en: They flee far from me, and spare not to spit in my face [10].

30.9.1.en: Here righteous Job stands out as a type of the Lord Christ, who said of Himself: "And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again" (Mk 10:34). "For he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on" (Lk 18:32).

30.9.2.en: * All the wicked flee from the holy Church, not with their feet, but by the marks of their practice. They flee far away, not from a place but by forsaking her. Since pride has a foundation in them, they scorn her with open blame. For spitting in the face is not only to belittle the righteous in their absence, but to lie against each one even in their presence. So the wicked mock them openly, and belittle them and heap curses upon them... But the holy Church (like Job) knows how to stand firm in the midst of sufferings, and to receive an honored life in the midst of insults. She learns not to be broken down by calamities, nor to boast in times of prosperity.

30.9.4.en: * Look at Christ, how many offenses He endured!

30.9.5.en: How that fool dared to spit in His face!

30.9.6.en: How did you dare, O tongue, to pour out spittle...?!

30.9.7.en: How did you endure, O earth, the mockery of the Son...?!

30.9.8.en: A fearful sight, filled with amazement, that a man should see the candle standing and spit in the face of the flame...

30.9.9.en: And this also happened for the sake of Adam, for he deserved the spitting because he had erred! And in place of the servant the Master arose to receive all!

30.9.10.en: He offered His face to receive the spittle, for He promised in Isaiah that He would not hide His face from shame and spitting...!

30.9.11.en: The Master (of Adam) had compassion on his weakness, and entered in to receive the shame in his place!

30.10.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh Because he hath loosed my cord, and afflicted me, they have also let loose the bridle before me [11].

30.10.1.en: Job portrays what happened as by the permission of God, whom he likens to one who looses the arrow toward the target, so that it struck Job and overcame him, or caused him a grave wound. It is as though what befell him was not chance but divine permission, even though he does not know the cause of God's anger against him.

30.10.2.en: And when God gave them the green light to do to Job what they pleased, they became like horsemen riding strong and violent horses, and they left the reins (the bridle) so that the horses would rush upon him with all their might.

30.10.3.en: With the bitterness of both pictures, Job nevertheless recognizes an important truth: that what befell him came only by God's permission, even though he does not know the cause of this permission.

30.10.4.en: * [And since God hath loosed his bowstring and brought me low] [11]. What does he mean by the bowstring of God but His secret counsel? Now the Lord shoots the arrow from the bowstring when He issues a judgment from His secret counsel. For we know that any man may be scourged, but for what cause the scourgings are issued, this we do not know. But after the scourging a correction takes place in life, and the power of the counsel is revealed. So the drawn bowstring is the hidden counsel. We are chastised by a loosed bowstring when, after the scourging, we perceive by what counsel we were struck.

30.10.5.en: The wicked took advantage of this divine permission and supposed that they were crushing Job without hindrance. They let their tongues mock Job without putting any bridle or limit upon them. But the children of God know when to speak and when to be silent. They use the bridle of silence with wisdom and prudence.

30.10.6.en: * [And he hath put a bridle in my mouth]... The saints see the bridle of silence placed upon them with regard to the hard hearts of lost sinners, when they say with the prophet: "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a strange land?" (Ps 4:137). Paul commanded the putting on of a bridle when he charged his disciple: "A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject" (Titus 10:3). So the holy teachers, often with heavenly knowledge, examine the hearts of those who oppose them, and when they see that these hearts have been left by God, they grieve and sigh, and are silent. Did not Solomon sometimes make a bridle for teachers when he says: "Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee" (Prov 8:9)...

30.10.7.en: The holy Church, which always offers her words in the spirit of love, sometimes halts her words for love's sake, and says: [Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth] (Ps 3:141).

30.11.0.en: Upon my right hand rise the youth (the base fellows), they push away my feet, and they raise up against me the ways of their destruction [12].

30.11.1.en: Some translations have: "On the right hand the youths rise." The Jesuit translation has: "The rabble rose up at my right hand, they make my feet stumble," and also: "They make my feet stumble, and pave the way to calamity."

30.11.2.en: Rising at the right hand is an expression used for bringing accusations against a person. So they rose against him with the violence of youth, set a snare for him, and lifted him up so that he would fall in it on his heel, and then trample him with their feet. The matter does not stop at false accusations, but with violence and force they cast him down and trample upon him.

30.11.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that rising against a person on the left signifies the opposition of enemies from outside, while rising against him on the right signifies the opposition of those who ought to have been his defenders, that is, opposition from within; and this is more dangerous and more bitter.

30.11.4.en: * Calamities are presented on the left if the Church meets an enemy who persecutes her at the hands of persons outside the fold of religion, those who deny Christ. But when she suffers troubles coming from persons who appear to be believers, enrolled under the name of Christ, and who oppose His name within her. In the same way the "right hand" is used for one whom we count great: "And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him" (Zech 1:3).

30.11.5.en: * [They make my feet stumble, and they press down with their paths as with waves] [12]. What does he mean by the feet of the Church but her members who are furthest away? They give themselves over to earthly works, and are quickly deceived by the enemies in proportion to their lack of understanding of heavenly things. Therefore the enemies make her feet stumble when they draw the furthest members into the errors of their teachings. The stumbling feet cannot keep the way, since all the weak are either deceived by the promises of the persecutors, or terrified by their threats, or broken by their torments, and thus they turn aside from the straight way.

30.12.1.en: The Catholic translation has: "And they cut off my way, and contribute to my destruction, and need no helper."

30.12.2.en: The work of the enemy of good and his wicked followers is to spend every effort in corrupting the way, by removing the signs, so that man loses his way and loses his peace during his journey.

30.12.3.en: * Let blessed Job speak these things concerning the evil spirits, the hidden enemies. Let the Catholic Church speak concerning the wicked persecutors, the visible enemies, for these cut off her way, when they oppose the souls of the weak on the ways of truth, obstructing them with deceit.

30.12.5.en: If the deceiver removes the signs of the way in order to mislead humanity and destroy it, the Savior has come to declare: "I am the way" (Jn 14:6), whom we acquire and in whom we walk, and so enjoy the Kingdom within us.

30.12.6.en: * This way is good; it leads the good man to the good Father, the man who brings forth good things out of his good treasure, the good and faithful servant (Mt 7:14; Lk 6:45; Mt 25:21). But this way is narrow, and the majority, who are mostly carnal, cannot travel in it. But the way is narrow also for those who strive to pass through it, since it was not said "it is confined" but narrow.

30.12.7.en: Origen the Scholar * Now the way cannot err, I mean Jesus Christ; for He says: "I am the way... and the life." This way leads to the Father, for He says, "no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (Jn 6:14).

30.12.8.en: St. Ignatius of Antioch They came upon me as a wide breaking in of waters.

30.13.0.en: In the desolation they rolled themselves upon me [14].

30.13.1.en: They come upon him like a wide stone crusher; however firm he may be, he will not escape them, but they will crush him. They do not walk toward him but roll swiftly like a destructive storm.

30.13.2.en: If the enemy of good appears as a stone crusher to crush humanity like stones thrown on the road, the Cornerstone has come down to us (Zech 4:7; Eph 2:20), to join us together in Himself and raise up from us a heavenly temple that the enemy cannot touch.

30.13.3.en: St. Augustine sees that by the calling of the Lord Christ, the cornerstone, who is the head of the Church, the Church is the corner that has joined the Jews on one side and the Gentiles on the other.

30.14.0.en: They pursue my soul as the wind: and my welfare passeth away as a cloud [15].

30.14.1.en: In a lamentation over his condition Job says that terrors have turned toward him and weighed upon him; they removed his honor (his soul's dignity) like a wind that blew it away, and his prosperity left him like a cloud that passed and vanished.

30.14.2.en: Job is amazed at what has happened, for this befalls the wicked who wither, when calamities come upon them and they lose their success and honor.

30.14.3.en: * [As the wind has driven away my desire... and as a cloud has my health passed] [15]. The cloud floats on high, and the breath of the wind draws it away as on a swift road. So surely will be the fate of the temporal goods of the wicked. They appear in the height of honor, to pass their life as those on high, but they soon come down daily in life, like those who are blown away along with their mortal life.

30.15.s.en: 3. His collapse in soul and body

30.15.0.en: 16 "And now my soul is poured out upon me; the days of affliction have taken hold upon me. 17 My bones are pierced in me in the night season: and my sinews take no rest. 18 By the great force of my disease is my garment changed: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat. 19 He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes. 20 I cry unto thee, and thou dost not hear me: I stand up, and thou regardest me not. 21 Thou art become cruel to me: with thy strong hand thou opposest thyself against me. 22 Thou liftest me up to the wind; thou causest me to ride upon it, and dissolvest my substance. 23 For I know that thou wilt bring me to death, and to the house appointed for all living. 24 Howbeit he will not stretch out his hand to the grave, though they cry in his destruction. 25 "Did not I weep for him that was in trouble? was not my soul grieved for the poor? 26 When I looked for good, then evil came unto me: and when I waited for light, there came darkness. 27 My bowels boiled, and rested not: the days of affliction prevented me. 28 I went mourning without the sun: I stood up, and I cried in the congregation. 29 I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls. 30 My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat. 31 My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep.

30.15.1.en: Now that Job has offered a lamentation bewailing his state, since God has directed His arrows against him, and the wicked have taken advantage of the situation and attacked him by every means, in merciless violence, and calamities have befallen him from every side, he now reveals the effect of all this on his psychological and physical health.

30.15.2.en: "And now my soul is poured out upon me; the days of affliction have taken hold upon me" [16].

30.15.3.en: Job sees the days of affliction, which have lasted so long, as having seized him and not let him go, so that his soul has collapsed and dried up completely.

30.15.4.en: * [Now my soul is dried up within me, the days of affliction have laid hold upon me] [16]. The souls of the elect are dried up now, so that afterward they become green in triumphant eternity.

30.15.5.en: Now the days of sorrow lay hold upon them, and the days of joy follow afterward. As it is written: [For him that feareth the Lord it shall go well at the last] (Sir 13:1).

30.15.6.en: Again it is said of the Church: [She shall rejoice in the last day] (Prov 25:31).

30.15.7.en: Now is the time of sorrow for the righteous, and a day will come when glory follows them instead of tears. It is said elsewhere: [Thou hast broken us in the place of sorrows] (Ps 19:44).

30.15.8.en: [The place of sorrows] is the present life; therefore the righteous man is crushed here, but in eternal life, the place of bliss, he is exalted.

30.15.9.en: But when he said, [The soul is dried up], he rightly began it with the words, [in myself]... For in ourselves our souls truly grieve, but in God they are refreshed.

30.16.0.en: My bones are pierced in me in the night season: and my sinews take no rest [17].

30.16.1.en: Here he speaks of the night as a person, as in Job (Job 3:3). The night plays a grave role: its work is to pierce his bones so that his skeleton collapses, and the sinews within him do not cease to send out the pain that gnaws at his being!

30.16.2.en: By the great force of my disease is my garment changed.

30.17.0.en: It bindeth me about as the collar of my coat [18].

30.17.1.en: Job lost the garments of honor, as a ruler and judge who had a role and a word in society, but what is more serious is that his clothes became tattered and altogether wretched because of the diseases and sores that befell his body. His outer garments turned into garments of perpetual mourning, or garments of grief, that encircled his body and do not leave him, like his inner garments.

30.17.2.en: * According to the historical interpretation, what does the garment of blessed Job mean if not his body? Truly the garment was worn out when his body was subjected to torment.

30.18.0.en: He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes [19].

30.18.1.en: In ancient times simple Easterners used to express their intense grief either by sitting on the dust, or by putting it on their heads as they mourned. Here Job pictures God as casting him into the dust to practice grief in its utmost form, and what increased his pain was that Job saw in himself that he had become like dust and ashes.

30.18.2.en: In any case, this lamentation bore an image of the contrition of soul and humility to which Job had come, since he counted himself dust and ashes. Abraham said: "Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27). And in Ben Sirach: "The Lord looketh on the host of high heaven; and all men are but dust and ashes" (Sir 17:31). So man looks at the truth of himself and finds himself dust, but in Christ Jesus he becomes a new creation after the image of his Creator.

30.18.3.en: * Scripture says: [I have despised myself, and cast myself down, and counted myself dust and ashes] (Job 19:30) (Vulgate). This is the humility of the penitent. When Abraham spoke with his God, and wished to discuss with Him the matter of the burning of Sodom, he said: "I am dust and ashes" (Gen 27:18). How is this humility always found in the great saints?

30.18.4.en: St. Augustine * O rich man, why do you exalt yourself with your wealth and boast of the glories of your forefathers? Do you boast of your homeland, take pleasure in the beauty of your body, and rejoice in a passing honor? Take heed to yourself. Remember that you are a mortal man [and that you are dust, and unto dust shalt thou return] (Gen 3:19)... Bow down and look at the tombs: can you distinguish between the bones of the poor and the bones of the rich? Between the bones of slaves and the bones of masters? Take heed to yourself, then, and give up pride, stinginess and hardness of heart.

30.18.5.en: St. Basil the Great * It is said of St. Anthony that when he entered the inner desert the demons looked at him and were troubled, and gathered against him and said to him: "O youth in age and mind, how did you dare to enter our land? For we have not seen here any human but you!" And they all began to fight him. He said to them: [O strong ones, what do you want from me, the weak and wretched? And what is my worth that you should all gather against me, when I am dust and filth and nothing, and too weak to fight one of your least?] And he would cast himself on the ground, and cry out and say: [O my Lord, help me and strengthen my weakness; have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have taken refuge in You; O Lord, do not forsake me, and let not those prevail against me who think that I am something; O Lord, You know that I am too weak to resist one of the least of these]. And whenever the demons heard this prayer, full of life and humility, they would flee from him and could not come near him.

30.18.6.en: The Garden of the Monks I cry unto thee, and thou dost not hear me.

30.19.0.en: I stand up, and thou regardest me not [20].

30.19.1.en: Often some believers, in the bitterness of their souls, feel as though God does not answer their prayers and cries. Yet He is called "thou that hearest prayer" (Ps 65:2). In His hearing of prayer, the answer may be the granting of the request, but at the fitting time. So it was in His answer to Abraham's request, when He gave him Isaac, but in the time of old age; and God may refuse the request because He knows that it is not for the good of the one who asks.

30.19.2.en: * When His saints suffer under the pressure of the persecution of enemies, and when they cry out without ceasing, beseeching Him to deliver them, by a great dispensation God seems as one who does not hear the voices of their supplications, so that they may be proved all the more in their sufferings.

30.19.3.en: They are proved all the more when their petition is not quickly answered... It is written: "O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not" (Ps 2:22).

30.19.5.en: * Do not grow weary in your asking. Do not think that your request returns empty.

30.19.6.en: Do not say: I have asked much and not found, and perhaps I shall never find.

30.19.7.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh Thou art become cruel to me.

30.20.0.en: With thy strong hand thou opposest thyself against me [21].

30.20.1.en: In the bitterness of his soul Job sees God as though He were harsh, using all the power of His hand against him. There is no proportion between the mighty power of God's hand and the weakness of man, so how can he bear to be opposed by God? The Jesuit translation has: "You have become a cruel enemy to me, and with the strength of Your hands You have attacked me."

30.20.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that God appears harsh or violent toward His saints, not because there is cruelty and violence in Him, but He appears so by opposing our will, and so we count Him such.

30.21.0.en: Thou liftest me up to the wind; thou causest me to ride upon it, and dissolvest my substance [22].

30.21.1.en: The Jesuit translation has: "You snatched me away, and made me ride upon the wind, and the tempest dissolved me." And the NKJ translation has: "You lift me up to the wind and cause me to ride upon it; you spoil my success."

30.21.2.en: Perhaps Job counted the days of his prosperity as though God had lifted him up to the wind, so that he became very high; the winds became his supreme chariot. But as high as he rose, God allowed him to fall, so that all he had gained is shattered!

30.21.3.en: Truly the passing glory of the world is vain glory; it is a sitting on the wind, which is unsafe, for the more a man counts himself as flying on the wind, the more his fall will be utterly destructive to him.

30.21.4.en: * The glory of the present life seems to be high, but there is no stability in it, so that man is like one who has been lifted up and seated on the wind (that is, without stability, but he falls from it).

30.22.0.en: For I know that thou wilt bring me to death, and to the house appointed for all living [23].

30.22.1.en: The men of the Old Testament looked toward death, which is the destiny of every man, as a passage to Hades, which is the house of every living one, his home to which he returns. But the Lord Christ came, and moved the believing dead from Hades to paradise, as spoils He rescued from the hand of the devil and from the dominion of eternal death.

30.22.2.en: * In the earlier part of this work I pointed out that before the coming of the Lord even the righteous went down to the dwellings of Hades, even though they were not fallen into woes but were at rest... Truly this was fitting for Job before the grace of the Savior, since the righteous were carried to the dwellings of Hades. The mere entering of Hades is called [the house of all the living].

30.22.4.en: Howbeit he will not stretch out his hand to the grave?

30.23.0.en: Though they cry in his destruction? [24]

30.23.1.en: The Catholic translation has: "Surely no hand is stretched out against ruin, and in collapse there comes help" [24].

30.23.2.en: A wonderful insight of righteous Job, and a living attitude of faith: while God's hand appears harsh to him, and God's actions come as from an enemy, he confesses that what God permits of temporal ruin is, as it were, God's hand for eternal edification. He looks at his calamity and perceives, as he cries for help, that it is for his salvation, even if it reaches temporary collapse.

30.23.3.en: * [In any case, thou wilt not stretch out thy hand to their ruin, and if they fall to the ground thou wilt rescue them thyself]. While Job tells of his circumstances and of others not being punished... he sees that the Lord does not stretch out His hand to the destruction of those who sin, when He corrects their condition by striking them.

30.23.5.en: Did not I weep for him that was in trouble?

30.24.0.en: Was not my soul grieved for the poor? [25]

30.24.1.en: With living faith righteous Job calls for divine intervention. He does not justify himself, but he believes that, as he showed compassion, and as he used to weep when he found a man in distress and pitied the condition of the poor, God will surely repay him this compassion with compassion, as though he were saying to God: [Your rule: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again](a). I offered every compassion to suffering, wounded souls, and every comfort to the poor; now my soul groans from wounds and needs divine comforts. Is it not my right to wrest them from You, O You who alone are righteous?

30.24.2.en: * Notice how he trained himself with regard to the sufferings of the body and its humiliation, for as he had never suffered anything of the kind, since he had always lived in abundant wealth and eminence, he was accustomed to take care of the misfortunes of others, one by one. This is what he declared when he said: "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me" (Job 25:3). Again: [Did I not weep for him that was in trouble? Was not my soul grieved when I saw a man in affliction?] (cf. Job 25:30). Because of this he was not troubled by anything that befell him.

30.24.3.en: * Let our mercies overflow, and let us give proofs of our great love for man, whether by using our money or our actions. If we see someone being abused and beaten in the marketplace, then if we can give money on his behalf, let us do so, or if we can save him by words, let us not hold back. For even offering a word has its reward, and even more our sighs. This is what Job said: [I wept for every man in distress, and I sighed when I saw a man in affliction] (Job 25:30).

30.24.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * [I have wept in times past for him that was in trouble; my soul was grieved with the poor] [25]. Although it is true compassion for us to share the sufferings of our fellow creature by giving generously, sometimes when outward goods are abundant with us, our hands give generously and more easily than we offer feelings of sharing in sorrow.

30.24.5.en: Therefore it is fitting for us to know that we give in a perfect manner when we reach those who suffer, and at the same time carry within us the same feelings as theirs.

30.24.6.en: It is fitting for us first to bear within us the sufferings of the person who suffers, and afterward to share his sorrows, showing our cooperation through practical service...

30.24.7.en: The compassion of our heart reaches perfection when we do not fear to lay upon ourselves the evil of need for the sake of our fellow, in order to rescue him from pain.

30.24.8.en: This model of compassion was in fact given to us by the Mediator between God and men. For He could have come to help us without dying, but He wished to help humanity by dying. Surely if He had not borne our wounds, His love for us would have been very little... He showed how great is the virtue of compassion by placing Himself in a state that He does not want us to be in, and this for our sake...

30.24.9.en: This too is what the holy Church should do. When she sees a person bearing the tears of repentance, she binds her tears to him with constant prayer, and sympathizes with the poor man in order to help the mind stripped of virtues by her supplications and intercession. We lament for the sorrowful, sympathizing with him, when we feel that the wounds of others are our wounds, and we strive with our tears to wash away the sins of those who commit transgression.

30.25.0.en: When I looked for good, then evil came unto me: and when I waited for light, there came darkness [26].

30.25.1.en: Job is amazed: he who was hoping for blessings in return for his compassion toward his brethren, and evils (trials) poured upon him. When he had lit the way for those around him, darkness surrounded him. He expected the shining of a bright morning upon his life, and found himself in deep night.

30.25.2.en: These are human feelings, even for men of God at times, when trials intensify upon them at a time when they were hoping for an abundance of blessings!

30.25.3.en: * The faithful hope for good but receive evil, and they wait for light and darkness comes upon them, because for the hope of obtaining the reward, to enjoy the joys of the angels, they are delivered into the hands of those who persecute them, even if its attainment is delayed a little here in the lower world.

30.25.5.en: My bowels boiled, and rested not.

30.26.0.en: The days of affliction prevented me [27].

30.26.1.en: It is a picture of the righteous, or of the Church, as suffering, sharing her Christ's cross. Within her is a ceaseless boiling, as she lives as in days of misery. As the psalmist says: [Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning](b).
